newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: India accord still haunts Sri Lanka one decade on.
newsitem.headline: India accord still haunts Sri Lanka one decade on.

text.p: A decade after Sri Lanka signed a controversial accord with neighbouring India, it is still grappling with a war against Tamil separatists and the ghost of a constitutional amendment.

The accord, signed by then Indian prime minister Rajiv Gandhi and Sri Lankan president Junius Jayawardene in the last week of July 1987, brought Indian troops to the island to disarm the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE).
It also led to the 13th amendment of the Sri Lankan constitution, under which the system of devolving more powers to newly created provincial councils was introduced.

The Indian Peace Keeping Forces (IPKF) lost more than 1,000 men in battles against the LTTE, who received support from Sri Lanka's United National Party government headed by Ranasinghe Premadasa, who opposed the accord with India.
"The IPKF episode played itself out. It was a bad episode altogether," Foreign Minister Lakshman Kadirgamar told Reuters in a recent interview.
Some 100,000 IPKF troops left Sri Lanka in early 1990, withdrawn by the government that followed Gandhi's after general elections in 1989.
But while most Sri Lankans consider the stay of the IPKF a bad memory, the political reality of provincial councils continues to haunt them as the government attempts to implement a new constitution.

The 13th amendment temporarily merged the Tamil-dominated north and Moslem dominated east into one provincial council pending a referendum on the issue. Ten years on, the merger has almost become permanent.
"The challenge now is to go beyond the devolution that India foisted upon us," columnist Paikashothy Sarvanamuttu said.

The devolution debate in Sri Lanka is as heated as the 14-year-old war with LTTE that has claimed more than 50,000 lives. The rebels are fighting for a separate homeland for minority Tamils in the north and east of the island.
The ruling Peple's Alliance says the draft constitution, currently being discussed by a parliamentary select committee, is one part of the politico-military solution to the ethnic conflict.
The other is military neutralisation of the LTTE.

The draft constitution, which is more federal in nature than the one in use, mentions key issues such as devolution of power to minorities and the demarcation of proposed new administrative councils in Sri Lanka's north and east, which would include a Moslem enclave.

Justice and Constitutional Affairs Minister Gamini Peiris, the architect of the new constitution, has called the 13th amendment a "sham" and "a response to external pressure that could not be resisted at that time".

But a delay in consensus between the government and the main opposition UNP over the draft constitution, has led most mainstream Tamil parties to cry out for making the earlier amendment a basis of the latest devolution proposals.
One of them, the Tamil United National Front, has also demanded the inclusion of the LTTE in discussions.
But Peiris is adamant. He has said that the government retains the option of a national referendum on the constitution if all political parties are unable to reach a consensus on the reforms.
"If all that fails, then the government will go to the people and ask them what they feel about it," he told a news conference earlier this month.
As politicians squabble, the war continues and it is possible the government will eventually have to fall back on what India helped introduce.
"It is not at all clear whether the devolution proposals are to tempt, tame or trounce the Tigers or accomplish all these feats all at once," said Sarvanamuttu.
"The irony of course is that Peiris' "sham" may prove to have been more implementable than his package so consciously designed with implementation in mind," he added.
